executive_summary: AUD/NZD closed at 1.23895 on 2026-10-02, meaning 1 AUD buys 1.23895 NZD; a rising quote means AUD is strengthening against NZD. The cross is up 1.20% over one month, 1.52% over three, 2.49% over six and 8.89% over twelve. It sits at the 94th percentile of its 52-week closing range, 67 pips below the 1.24567 closing high. The main bilateral story is a 185bp policy gap (RBA 4.60%, RBNZ 2.75%) with both central banks hiking, but the market prices their next moves very differently. The RBNZ's 28 October hike is about 75% priced and the RBA's 3 November hike only about 20%. That asymmetry, plus a core-inflation gap of about 90bp (Australian trimmed mean 3.6% vs RBNZ sectoral core 2.7%), produces a tactical Bullish verdict at conviction 3 with a net score of +0.2999. The two dossiers reinforce each other on that horizon: AUD scores Bullish on its own at +0.304 and NZD Bearish at −0.159. Over one to six months the verdict flips to Bearish at conviction 3 (−0.2344). Neither dossier's dollar-based score shows this, because it rests on two purely bilateral features: the RBNZ is converging on the RBA, and Australia's real exchange rate is 13 points richer while it runs the larger external deficit. Sell-side views are already bearish on the cross: BofA's forecast deck has AUD/NZD at 1.20 for Q4 2026 and 1.18 in Q1 and Q2 2027, and an aggregator consensus puts Q4 2026 at 1.2142. The caveat on the tactical call is real. The edge depends on one release, the 28 October Australian CPI. The chart has made lower highs under the 1.24921 52-week high since 22 September, and the RBA's 29 September hike produced no upside follow-through. We would therefore build the tactical long on dips toward 1.2300 rather than chase it at spot, and hand over to the strategic short after 3 November.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On World Bank 2025 PPP conversion factors, both dossiers put fair value at about 1.0529, so spot is roughly 17.7% rich. That is the largest PPP gap of any AUD cross outside the Balassa-Samuelson cases. The real exchange rates point the same way. The BIS REER is 116.11 for Australia (August, up 9.97% on the year and the highest in the G10+SGD set) and 102.84 for New Zealand (flat on the year, 44th percentile of its cached history). The 13.3-point REER gap has opened almost entirely from the Australian side. So the current level prices the RBA's 185bp policy advantage plus a terms-of-trade premium tied to the energy shock. Goldman's view was that the cross screens rich against rate differentials, credit spreads, VIX and crude in its GSBEER framework but is broadly justified by the macro regime. RBC questions the energy part of that story: it notes Australia posted its first trade deficit in almost a decade this year, largely on higher energy import costs, and warns that refined-oil disruptions bode poorly for AUD. That cuts against the 'oil up → pair up' netting in Factor 5, and is flagged as a live disagreement rather than a settled point. Valuation is not actionable inside four weeks. On a one-to-six month view it is a headwind with no floor nearby. Spot is at the 94th percentile of the 52-week closing range (92nd intraday), 67 pips below the closing high of 1.24567 and 9.90% above the 52-week low; Goldman described the cross as at its highest level in more than a decade as early as May, and spot is higher now.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral policy differential is +185bp, with the RBA Cash Rate Target at 4.60% after a unanimous 25bp increase on 29 September and the RBNZ Official Cash Rate at 2.75% after its 25bp increase on 2 September. That gap is the widest bilateral policy spread in the dollar bloc and it pays the long side of the pair. The question for four weeks is not the level but the surprise relative to pricing, and the two legs are priced very differently. The RBNZ's 28 October decision carries roughly a 75% probability of a 25bp move to 3.00%, which means the 25bp of compression is substantially discounted already; the quote dossier's own estimate of 70% is essentially in line, so there is little edge in the New Zealand leg. The Australian leg is the opposite: roughly 20% and about 7bp of a 25bp step are discounted for 3 November, against the base dossier's assessment of about 45%. Mechanically the market's expected change in the differential over the window is about -13.75bp, while the dossiers' own probabilities imply about -6.25bp, so the expected realised compression is roughly 7.5bp less than the curve carries. Transmission is direct: Australian front-end repricing of 10-18bp on an upside trimmed-mean print widens the gap against a New Zealand leg that cannot reprice much further. Add the carry itself, worth roughly 15-19 pips a month depending on whether the policy differential or the realised roll premium is used, and the four-week balance tilts to the pair rising even though the modal path is a modest narrowing.

tactical.what_is_priced: The curve prices the RBNZ as moving on 28 October and the RBA as finished, so the compression is largely in and the expansion is barely in. The asymmetry of surprise, not the direction of the modal path, is where the four-week edge sits.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the direction of travel compresses the differential, and both dossiers reach that conclusion independently. The RBNZ is early in a cycle that began from 2.25% in July, with a published track peaking at 3.28% and bank paths running from 3.25% to 3.50% by March 2027 and one house as high as 4.00% by September 2027. The RBA sits at 4.60% with a labour market at a post-COVID high of 4.6% unemployment and business conditions negative for the first time since September 2020, which caps the cycle at 4.60-4.85%. On the modal path the gap narrows from 185bp toward 135-160bp, and the datable mechanism is the sequence of scheduled decisions in the gated calendar: RBNZ 28 October, RBA 3 November, RBA 8 December and RBNZ 9 December, with the RBNZ's December meeting carrying a Monetary Policy Statement and therefore a new published track while the RBA's two decisions carry no projection-round note in that file. The important qualification is that convergence is already substantially discounted in the curve: the Australian 2-year at about 4.98-5.00% against the New Zealand 2-year at 3.92% gives a bilateral front-end gap of roughly 106-108bp, and the 10-year cross-section gap is only about 28bp, both far inside the 185bp policy differential. So the strategic edge is not the direction of convergence, which is priced, but its speed, and the one scheduled projection round in the window belongs to the bank with the upgrade to deliver. That skews delivery risk toward faster compression than the curve assumes, which is why the stance is Bearish and why the confidence is only 53.

strategic.what_is_priced: The front end already discounts about 77bp of the 185bp differential closing, so the market agrees on direction. factors.horizon_split: The stances diverge because pricing and trajectory point opposite ways. Over four weeks the compression is already 75% discounted in the RBNZ leg while the expansion is only 20% discounted in the RBA leg, so the surprise asymmetry favours the pair rising even though the modal path narrows the gap. Over one to three months the modal path is the whole story: the RBNZ keeps moving after the RBA stops, and the only scheduled projection round in the window belongs to the RBNZ. The inflection is the 28 October to 3 November pair of decisions, after which the tactical pricing asymmetry is spent and only the trajectory remains.

carry_analysis.carry_regime: Carry is a genuine ranking signal for this cross rather than a rounding error, which distinguishes it from most AUD and NZD pairs against the dollar. A 185bp differential on a cross whose realised volatility is only 4.73% is the second-best carry-to-volatility combination available to an AUD holder after AUD/CHF, and the lowest-volatility way to own the differential inside the dollar bloc. The regime caveat is that the carry is being paid precisely because the market expects it to shrink: the 2-year gap of roughly 108bp is already 77bp inside the policy gap, so the holder is being compensated for convergence risk rather than receiving a free differential.
carry_analysis.breakeven_move: At the 185bp policy differential on a 1.23895 spot the long side accrues roughly 0.00191 a month, about 19 pips, so the pair can fall by about that much over thirty days before the carry is erased. Both figures are material relative to a cross whose realised volatility is under 5%, which is the mechanical reason this pair is cheap to hold in either direction and why conviction, not carry, should size it.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The headline inflation rates are almost identical and the core rates are not, and the core gap is what matters for the pair. Australian headline monthly CPI re-accelerated to 4.0% year-on-year in August from 3.5% in July with the RBA trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% for a third consecutive month, while New Zealand's June-quarter headline was 4.1% but the RBNZ sectoral factor core was 2.7%, the 30% trimmed mean 2.6% and the weighted median 2.7%. Australia therefore has roughly 90bp more underlying inflation on the measures each central bank actually targets, and New Zealand's overshoot is explicitly tradables-driven, with petrol up 20.1% and diesel up 47.7% in the quarter against non-tradables easing to 3.4%. The labour markets differ by a full percentage point in the same direction: Australian unemployment 4.6% against New Zealand 5.6%, the latter the highest since September 2015. Both economies print quarterly CPI inside the window, New Zealand on 21 October and Australia on 28 October, but their repricing capacity is asymmetric because the Australian print feeds a decision discounted at 20% while the New Zealand print feeds one discounted at 75%. The transmission is therefore through the relative policy response rather than through growth: a firm Australian trimmed mean has far more room to move the differential than an equally firm New Zealand headline. Confidence is held under 50 because both prints carry genuine two-sided risk and because Australian growth momentum is the weaker of the two on the survey evidence.

What it does not price symmetrically is the response function: the Australian core print can move a 20%-discounted decision, the New Zealand print can only confirm a 75%-discounted one.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the macro differential converges rather than widens, which removes the directional signal. On the Australian side the deterioration is documented and fresh: NAB quarterly business conditions turned negative at -2 for the first time since September 2020, sales margins fell to -20, purchase costs rose 1.2% in the quarter against final product prices of 0.5%, the composite PMI fell to 50.8 and unemployment is on a path the base dossier puts at 4.8-5.0% by the March quarter. On the New Zealand side the deterioration has already largely happened: unemployment at 5.6% with the RBNZ projecting only a marginal dip to 5.5%, real gross national disposable income down 0.4% in the quarter, house prices flat to falling and activity expectations in the ANZ survey degrading within September from 52 early in the month to 36 late. So the unemployment gap of 100bp narrows as Australia's rises toward a level New Zealand has already reached, and the core inflation gap of 90bp narrows only slowly as Australian trimmed mean drifts toward 3.2-3.5% and New Zealand core toward the middle of its band. Neither economy is the clear relative loser over the horizon and the offsetting trajectories cancel. The honest reading is that this factor has no strategic directional content for the cross and should not be made to carry one.

factors.horizon_split: The split is mechanical and turns on which quantity matters at which horizon. Over four weeks the level of the core inflation gap matters because it determines whose CPI print can move a lightly discounted policy decision, and Australia wins that comparison by roughly 90bp of core and a 20%-versus-75% pricing asymmetry. Over one to three months the trajectory matters more than the level, and both gaps close from the Australian side as unemployment rises toward where New Zealand's already is, which cancels the stance into Neutral.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: AUD/NZD is a low risk-beta cross by the framework's own classification: both legs are high-beta, commodity-linked, dollar-funded Antipodean currencies whose global risk betas largely net out, leaving the factor with far less bilateral content than it has for a pair with a haven on one side. Reduced -0.03 tactically and -0.02 strategically, redeployed to Factors 1 and 5.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the factor with the least bilateral content on the whole pair, because the two legs sit on the same side of almost every risk axis. Both are small, open, commodity-linked, dollar-funded currencies with high beta to global equities and to Chinese demand, so a generalised risk-off move sells both and a risk-on move buys both. The cross-asset backdrop is mixed rather than directional: the VIX at 16.07 is at the 28th percentile of its one-year range, the S&P 500 is up roughly 14% over twelve months and almost unchanged on the month, while credit has begun to cheapen with US high yield at 302bp after a 42bp widening and investment grade at 83bp, both near the wider end of their one-year ranges. The one structural differentiator is depth rather than direction: New Zealand is the smaller and less liquid market, has no standing Fed swap line and must fund a persistent external deficit from abroad, so a disorderly funding event would plausibly hit the quote leg harder than the base leg. That is a tail observation, not a four-week stance, and quantifying it would require leaning on the cross's own recent trading, which this pass does not permit. Neutral is the correct output.

tactical.what_is_priced: Equity volatility prices continuation of a benign regime while credit has begun to price the rates shock. Neither signal discriminates between two currencies that sit on the same side of the risk trade, so there is nothing for the cross to express.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the same cancellation holds and the two identifiable regime shifts both affect the legs in the same direction. A Hormuz settlement that collapses the energy premium is risk-positive and growth-positive for both economies, lifting Chinese demand for Australian iron ore and New Zealand dairy alike while removing the imported inflation impulse from both central banks. A credit-led risk-off with high yield through 400bp sells both currencies. The one channel that genuinely discriminates is China, and it discriminates only weakly: the NBS manufacturing PMI returned to expansion at 50.1 in September, which matters more for Australian steel inputs than for New Zealand protein exports, so a Chinese stimulus impulse is the one risk-regime development with a cleanly pair-positive sign. Against that, the energy complex is the channel that runs the other way, and it belongs to Factor 5 rather than here. With the two most likely regime shifts affecting both legs in the same direction and only the China channel discriminating, the strategic stance is Neutral and the weight has been cut to 0.03 to reflect how little the factor can say about this particular cross.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Speculative accounts are short both legs on the aggregate measure, which mutes the pair signal by construction. For the 22 September report date the Australian legacy non-commercial net was short 46,814 contracts on open interest of 306,488, or roughly 15% of open interest, while the New Zealand all-spec net was short 11,380 on open interest of 101,377, or roughly 11%. In proportional terms the Australian short is modestly the larger, which if anything is a mild contrarian positive for the cross, but the Australian data contradicts itself: the disaggregated Traders in Financial Futures report for the same date shows leveraged funds net LONG 58,726 contracts against asset managers net short 55,353, and that divergence is unresolved. A positioning factor whose base-leg level cannot be established cannot carry a tactical stance. The direction of travel is cleaner and points mildly pair-positive: the Australian legacy net shortened in each of three successive reports while New Zealand asset managers swung 21,655 contracts short in a single week, so both cohorts were selling, with the New Zealand selling more abrupt. Set against that, Australian open interest collapsed 37.8% in a week to 306,488, which removes the leverage that would amplify any squeeze on the base leg. The structural flow cited for Australia, superannuation funds raising FX hedge ratios, is an AUD-versus-USD flow and does not transmit to this cross. Neutral at low confidence is the honest output.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months positioning in the two legs offers no directional signal for the cross and the data quality problem does not improve. Neither leg is at an extreme: the Australian legacy net short of 46,814 is roughly 58% of the plus-or-minus 80,000-contract threshold historically associated with reversals, and the New Zealand net short of 11,380 sits well inside both the plus-or-minus 30,000 zone treated as notable and the roughly 39,600-contract short reached as recently as August, implying about 28,000 contracts of extension capacity on the quote leg. Because neither side is crowded, neither side can lead. The pair-specific flow dynamic that would matter, a distinct trans-Tasman carry community positioned in the cross itself, is not observable in CFTC data, which covers each leg against the dollar and not the cross. Australian superannuation hedging and New Zealand dairy export receipts are both real structural flows, but they are both dollar-denominated channels and they do not net into a trans-Tasman direction. The reasonable expectation is that positioning amplifies whatever the rate and terms-of-trade factors deliver rather than leading them.

strategic.what_is_priced: Neither leg carries a crowded position, so there is no overhang to unwind and no squeeze to fade in the cross. Positioning is an amplifier here, not a driver.

factors.horizon_split: Aligned at Neutral with identical confidence on both horizons. The reason is the same at both: the base leg's positioning level is contradicted between two CFTC report families and cannot be established, and neither leg is at an extreme that would let direction be inferred from level. The tactical direction of travel, both cohorts selling, is too weak and too mutual to carry a stance.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Specs are short both legs, so the combined pair signal is muted rather than amplified. On a proportional basis the base-leg short (about 15% of open interest) modestly exceeds the quote-leg short (about 11%), which is a weak contrarian positive for the cross, but the base-leg disaggregated data shows a 58,726-contract leveraged long on the same report date and cancels the inference.
tactical.unwind_trigger: A dated double on 28 October: an Australian September-quarter trimmed mean at or above 3.7% forcing base-leg shorts to cover into a 3 November decision discounted at 20%, against a New Zealand decision the same day that is already 75% discounted and therefore has little covering left to generate. The opposite trigger is a soft Australian print alongside a hawkish RBNZ track, which would cover the quote-leg short instead.
tactical.historical_analogue: The August 2026 New Zealand episode, in which roughly 50,000 contracts of speculative short covering ran from about -39,600 to +10,500 within weeks. That demonstrates the quote leg's capacity to squeeze hard from a modest base, and it is the specific reason a cross-level contrarian read cannot be taken from the base leg alone.
tactical.contrarian_case: The case against a tactically bullish cross is that the base-leg short of 46,814 contracts is positioned correctly rather than carelessly: it is short a currency whose central bank faces a post-COVID-high unemployment rate and negative business conditions, and a soft 28 October trimmed mean vindicates it immediately, at which point those shorts add rather than cover while the quote leg is being supported by a delivered RBNZ hike.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Neither leg is crowded, so over one to three months positioning neither supports nor threatens the cross. The base leg sits at roughly 58% of its historical reversal threshold and the quote leg has about 28,000 contracts of room before reaching its own recent extreme.
strategic.unwind_trigger: On the strategic horizon the relevant unwind is of the base-leg leveraged long rather than of either short: if the 58,726-contract figure is the true exposure, the crowded trade is long the highest policy rate in the set, and an RBA pivot signalled through rising unemployment would unwind it against a quote currency whose central bank is still tightening.
strategic.historical_analogue: Asset managers reached record net-long and gross-long Australian dollar exposure several times in the months to May 2026. If that overhang persists it is a strategic supply of base-leg selling with no equivalent on the quote side, which is the positioning shape most consistent with the strategic rate-convergence view.
strategic.contrarian_case: The case against a strategically bearish cross is that the quote leg is the one with slow money actively selling into weakness, having swung 21,655 contracts short in a single week, and slow-money selling into a hiking central bank is the classic setup for a squeeze that runs further and faster than the rate convergence it is supposedly anticipating. A hawkish 9 December track upgrade that arrives after shorts have already extended would amplify the move, not cause it.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Commodity-versus-commodity pair with opposite energy signs: Australia is a net energy exporter through coal and LNG while New Zealand is a net energy importer, and the dominant global shock in the period is an oil price up roughly 50% over twelve months. That makes the terms-of-trade channel materially more informative for this cross than the default weight allows. Raised +0.03 on both horizons, funded from Factors 10 and 3.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Inside four weeks the commodity complex pulls the two legs in opposing directions hard enough to cancel, which is also the conclusion each dossier reaches for its own leg. On the Australian side iron ore at USD 96.59 a tonne is down 7.14% over twelve months and the June-quarter terms of trade fell 1.6%, but Newcastle thermal coal at USD 145.20 is up 36.72% and copper up 35.84%, with the RBA commodity price index up 15.5% year-on-year. On the New Zealand side the terms of trade fell 9.0% in a single quarter against a 2.2% expected fall, driven by import prices up 13.8% on fuel, but dairy is firm: Fonterra lifted its 2026/27 farmgate midpoint to NZD 9.50 per kilogram of milk solids and the August trade deficit of NZD 1.35bn beat an NZD 1.78bn estimate with exports up 15.4% year-on-year. Brent has retraced roughly 15% in eight sessions from USD 114.89 to the high nineties, which relieves the New Zealand import bill and erodes the Australian coal premium at the same time. The scheduled events inside the window are two GDT auctions on 6 and 20 October and the Australian international trade price indexes on 29 October, and none of them has a predictable sign. The direct bilateral trade channel is small and stable: Australia runs a USD 3.0bn goods surplus with New Zealand on USD 8.3bn of exports against USD 5.3bn of imports, a persistent but slow-moving pair-positive settlement flow that does not move inside four weeks.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices dairy at current levels, iron ore as range-bound and oil near the high nineties. With the energy retracement helping the quote leg and hurting the base leg's coal premium simultaneously, there is no four-week directional edge in the cross.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the levels dominate the quarterly shocks, and on levels the Australian external position is the weaker of the two. Australia's current account deficit widened by AUD 1.8bn to AUD 27.2bn, or 3.67% of GDP, with the balance on goods and services itself in deficit at AUD 5.1bn and net foreign debt at AUD 1,486.0bn; New Zealand's deficit narrowed to 3.2% of GDP, or 3.26% on the OECD vintage, helped by a smaller primary income deficit and a services balance back in surplus. So the base leg runs the larger deficit and has the worse decomposition, a commodity exporter running a goods and services deficit at the top of a terms-of-trade shock. The valuation overlay compounds it rather than offsetting it: the BIS real effective exchange rate is 116.11 for Australia, the highest in the benchmarking set and up 9.97% over twelve months, against 102.84 for New Zealand, flat on the year at the 44th percentile of its cached history, and World Bank PPP conversion factors put the cross roughly 15-18% expensive on fair value. The trajectory also favours the quote leg: the New Zealand terms-of-trade loss is a realised shock with oil already retracing and dairy being revised up, while Australia's principal export price is falling and the coal strength that offsets it is both a smaller export share and cyclically rather than structurally driven. The offsetting risk is Chinese stimulus from the December Central Economic Work Conference, which would reset iron ore and is the single cleanest pair-positive event in the window.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices the Australian rate advantage and does not price an external adjustment at all: a real effective exchange rate up 9.97% against falling iron ore and a goods and services deficit is the configuration the exchange rate usually resolves. The quote leg's shock, by contrast, is realised and retracing.

factors.horizon_split: The stance flips because the horizons weigh flows and levels differently. Inside four weeks the quarterly shocks offset: New Zealand's 9.0% terms-of-trade fall is worse than Australia's 1.6%, but Brent is retracing and dairy is being revised up while iron ore is flat, so nothing nets. Over one to three months cumulative balance-of-payments flows and real exchange rates set the price, and on those the base leg runs the larger deficit with the worse decomposition at a real exchange rate 13 points richer, which the quote leg does not. The signpost that would flip it back is Chinese stimulus resetting iron ore.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Australia: iron ore roughly 35% of export revenue at USD 96.59 a tonne and down 7.14% over twelve months; Newcastle thermal coal USD 145.20 and up 36.72%; LNG a major earner into a Hormuz-driven JKM shock; copper up 35.84%. Net energy EXPORTER in value terms through coal and LNG, so higher energy prices are a mild terms-of-trade positive offset by a weak iron ore complex.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: New Zealand: dairy roughly a quarter of goods exports, with the GDT index mixed at +0.9% then -1.1% in September and Fonterra's 2026/27 farmgate midpoint raised to NZD 9.50/kgMS; meat and forestry secondary. Net energy IMPORTER with no domestic oil of consequence, so the fuel bill is a direct charge on national income, visible in import prices up 13.8% in one quarter.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Applying the framework direction rules to the dominant shock. Oil up: Australia gets a mild positive (+) as a net energy exporter whose coal and LNG prices rise with it; New Zealand gets a clear negative as a pure energy importer, confirmed by import prices up 13.8% and a 9.0% terms-of-trade fall in one quarter. Net effect of higher oil is that the base leg gains relative to the quote leg, so the pair RISES. Natural gas and LNG up: Australia strongly positive through LNG and the coal substitution the IEA documents; New Zealand negative through imported fuel. Pair rises. Iron ore up: Australia strongly positive (++), New Zealand neutral to mildly positive through the same Chinese demand impulse that lifts dairy. Pair rises, but less than the raw rule implies because the China channel partly offsets. Dairy up: New Zealand strongly positive (++), Australia neutral. Pair FALLS. Netting the current state, energy is up roughly 50% over twelve months while iron ore is down 7.14% and dairy is firm but not surging, so the realised configuration has been mildly pair-positive on energy, pair-negative on iron ore and pair-negative on dairy, which is why the tactical stance nets to Neutral. The strategic sign is set by the retracement already under way in energy, which removes the one commodity axis working for the base leg. Pass-2 note (unscored): outside research on the oil sign is split. Goldman frames relative terms of trade as the dominant driver and as favouring Australia over New Zealand, which supports the netting above. RBC's warning that refined-oil disruption is AUD-negative says Australia's net energy position is weaker than the 'exporter' label implies. The scored stance stands as issued; the 'oil up → pair up' leg of the netting is lower-confidence than the 'oil down → pair down' leg.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair rises. Australia gains mildly through coal, LNG and the broader energy complex while New Zealand's import bill worsens directly, deepening a terms-of-trade loss already running at 9.0% a quarter and widening a current account deficit the quote dossier's cited forecast already has heading toward 4.5% of GDP. The second-order effect reinforces it: a higher oil price keeps both central banks hiking, but the RBNZ is hiking defensively into 5.6% unemployment while the RBA is hiking into 4.6%, so the base leg's policy response is the more sustainable one.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair falls. New Zealand's import bill falls directly and its realised terms-of-trade loss begins to reverse, while Australia loses the coal and LNG premium that has been offsetting weak iron ore, with Newcastle coal's 36.72% annual gain the component most exposed. The policy second-order effect also runs pair-negative: lower energy undermines the 'permanently higher' fuel premise behind the RBA's September hike more than it undermines the RBNZ's, because New Zealand's core inflation at 2.7% is already inside the band and its hikes are about removing stimulus rather than about fuel.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Brent crude, acting as the energy term in both legs with opposite signs. Iron ore is the larger single determinant of Australian export revenue and dairy of New Zealand's, but those two move on broadly the same Chinese demand impulse and therefore partly cancel in the cross, whereas oil enters the base leg as a revenue item through coal and LNG substitution and the quote leg as a cost item. Oil is the one commodity whose move has an unambiguous sign for AUD/NZD.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are communicating hawkishly, so the bilateral question is which one's guidance is further ahead of its own market pricing. On the Australian side the 29 September statement was unanimous, judged that a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted and retained the hiking option explicitly, while Governor Bullock declined formal forward guidance but said the Board will raise rates again if needed, described the fuel price increase as permanently higher and named the exchange rate the most important channel of transmission. Against that the market discounts roughly 20% and about 7bp of a 25bp step for 3 November. On the New Zealand side Governor Breman said persistent oil prices would push near-term inflation above the September assumptions, and the market responded by moving October hike pricing from about 30% to about 75%, which is now well ahead of the RBNZ's own published track peak of 3.28%. So the New Zealand guidance gap has already closed from the market side, while the Australian one has not: pricing sits at roughly a fifth of the stated option. A central bank that identifies the exchange rate as its principal transmission channel also has no incentive to talk its currency down, which is a directly pair-relevant asymmetry. The transmission into the cross is through the 10-18bp of Australian front-end repricing that an upside trimmed mean would force, against a New Zealand front end with little room left.

tactical.what_is_priced: The quote leg's hawkishness is fully in the price and then some, running ahead of the RBNZ's own track. The base leg's stated hiking option is discounted at about a fifth of its probability, and that gap is the bilateral asymmetry.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the communication asymmetry reverses, and the gated meeting calendar is the reason. The RBNZ's 9 December decision carries a Monetary Policy Statement, which is a full projection round with a new published OCR track, and the track currently peaks at 3.28% against bank paths of 3.25-3.50% and market front-end pricing that already exceeds it. That is a scheduled vehicle for an upward revision. The RBA's two decisions inside the window, 3 November and 8 December, carry no projection-round note in the gated file, so the base leg has no equivalent scheduled mechanism for extending its guidance even if the Board wished to. The credibility direction also diverges. The RBNZ moved from a 3-3 split decided on the Governor's casting vote in May to two hikes and a unanimous September decision, which is a bank building hawkish credibility from a low base. The RBA has already spent its hawkish credibility and now carries reversal risk: a Board that has told the market it will keep hiking has more to lose from stopping, and with unemployment at 4.6% and rising and business conditions negative for the first time since 2020, the probability it has to soften its own stated reaction function inside the window is not small. Confidence is held at 46 because this channel is substantially correlated with Factor 1 and should not be allowed to double-count the same convergence.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices the base leg's hawkishness as having peaked and the quote leg's as still building, which is broadly right. What is not priced is the scheduling asymmetry: only one of the two banks has a projection round inside the window at which to formalise a higher path.

factors.horizon_split: Confidence falls and the sign flips because the two horizons test different things. Over four weeks the test is which bank's stated intention is further ahead of its own market pricing, and that is unambiguously the RBA at roughly 20% against an explicitly retained option. Over one to three months the test is which bank has a scheduled mechanism to extend its guidance, and in the gated calendar only the RBNZ does, through the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement. The mechanism that erodes the tactical positive is simply its own resolution on 3 November.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Inside four weeks the event set is dense but symmetric for the cross. The Hormuz binary dominates and it cuts across both legs: a negotiated reopening collapses the energy premium, which relieves New Zealand's import bill and undermines the RBA's permanently-higher fuel premise at the same time, while an escalation does the reverse, so neither outcome has a clean pair sign. Middle East crude exports have recovered to roughly 80% of pre-war volumes, Iran's seven-day reopening proposal was rejected but talks at the UN General Assembly were described as productive with sequencing the sticking point, so the binary is live and near-dated. The one genuinely asymmetric item, the New Zealand general election on 7 November, falls just outside the tactical window, and the September Taxpayers' Union-Curia poll projected the governing bloc at 64 seats against 56, which limits the pre-positioning premium. Australia has no federal election due until May 2028 and no domestic political risk of consequence. The China channel transmits to both legs in the same direction, through steel demand for the base leg and dairy demand for the quote leg. With the dominant binary two-sided and the one asymmetric event outside the window, Neutral is correct.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices the war as a persistent background condition rather than an imminent binary, and prices the New Zealand election as a close but orderly contest. Both readings look fair and neither creates a four-week edge in the cross.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the single clean bilateral asymmetry appears: one leg of this pair faces a national election and a post-election fiscal reset inside the window and the other faces nothing. The New Zealand general election on 7 November is close enough that coalition formation under MMP could run into late November, and the December Half-Year Economic and Fiscal Update is the first fiscal forecast afterwards, so the quote leg carries both a political and a fiscal uncertainty premium that the base leg does not. Australia's calendar inside the window contains no election and a December Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook that is a low-impact update against a 1.6%-of-GDP deficit and an affirmed triple-A. Against that, the Hormuz binary remains two-sided for the cross for the reasons set out tactically, and Chinese policy events, the December Central Economic Work Conference in particular, transmit pair-positive through iron ore but partly offset through dairy demand. The net is a modest Bullish tilt driven almost entirely by the election asymmetry, which is why the confidence is only 45: a close election with the incumbent bloc ahead on seats is a thin basis for a directional stance, and a decisive result would remove the premium quickly.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices a close New Zealand election with limited currency consequence and an oil premium that persists. The election premium is the one piece that is genuinely one-sided for this cross and it is only partly reflected.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Neutral to Bullish purely on calendar placement. The New Zealand election falls on 7 November, outside a four-week tactical window from the valuation date but squarely inside the one-to-three month strategic one, and it is the only identified event in the whole set with an unambiguous bilateral sign. Everything else, principally Hormuz, is two-sided for the cross on both horizons, which is why strategic confidence is only 45.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: There is a real and durable fiscal differential between these two sovereigns but no mechanism by which it moves the cross inside four weeks. Australia holds Aaa from Moody's and AAA from S&P and Fitch, all stable, with net general government debt of 18.8% of GDP and an underlying cash balance of -1.6% of GDP; New Zealand holds Aaa from Moody's but AA+ from S&P and Fitch, with net core Crown debt projected to peak at 46.1% of GDP in 2027/28 and an OBEGALx surplus not forecast until 2028/29. That is roughly 27 percentage points of net debt and a one-notch ratings gap in Australia's favour. Neither sovereign faces a rating review, an auction event or a fiscal release inside the tactical window; the New Zealand Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update was published on 29 September, before the window opens. Both long ends have risen with the global move rather than on any domestic credit event, and neither carries a sovereign risk premium against the other. The honest tactical reading is that the differential is real, well known and not currently material, so the factor is not currently a price-setter for the cross.

tactical.what_is_priced: Both sovereigns are priced as high-grade credits with no differential premium in cash bonds despite a 27-point net debt gap. Nothing in the window changes that, so the factor takes no tactical stance.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the fiscal differential acquires a transmission channel, and it runs mildly in the base leg's favour. The channel is twofold. First, the regime: global long ends are repricing sovereign quality, with the US ten-year at the top of its one-year range and the UK the highest in the benchmarking set, and in that environment the sovereign with 18.8% net debt and three triple-A ratings is the one with more room rather than less. Australia also retains greater counter-cyclical capacity to offset the slowdown its own central bank is engineering, which lowers the tail risk on its asset prices relative to a sovereign whose debt is peaking near 46% and whose surplus is three years away. Second, the calendar: New Zealand has an election on 7 November followed by a Half-Year Economic and Fiscal Update in December, and the quote dossier notes that the Budget forecasts were built on lower yields and lower oil, so the surplus date is likely to be pushed out. A Labour-led outcome would loosen policy further. Australia's December Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook is a low-impact update by comparison. Confidence is held at 52 because this is a second-order channel and because Australian commodity revenue, the swing factor in its budget outcomes, is deteriorating with iron ore down 7.14% over twelve months.

strategic.what_is_priced: Ratings and cash spreads price both sovereigns as high grade and price no differential at all. In a regime actively discriminating on fiscal quality that under-prices the base leg's balance sheet advantage at the margin, though only at the margin.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Neutral to Bullish because fiscal quality works through a slow channel. Inside four weeks there is no rating action, no supply event and no scheduled fiscal release for either sovereign, so a 27-point debt gap changes nothing. Over one to three months the same gap determines relative counter-cyclical capacity in a regime that is repricing sovereign balance sheets, and the quote leg additionally faces an election and a post-election fiscal reset that the base leg does not.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This pass is deliberately not given the cross's chart, so the structural evidence available is limited to what the direction payload carries and the factor is scored accordingly. The volatility picture is the usable part. The estimated three-month at-the-money implied volatility is 5.476% at a 99.7-day tenor and 5.576% at 36.7 days, a very slightly inverted front, against realised sixty-day volatility of 4.73% reported in both dossiers. Implied above realised by roughly 0.75 of a volatility point is consistent with an event premium for the 21 and 28 October cluster, but the implied figure is a triangle estimate built from a realised correlation of 0.7833 rather than a quote, and the method has understated direct quotes by 8.7% to 17.8% in prior checks, so the gap to realised is probably wider than stated and may be the largest part of the signal. In absolute terms this remains one of the lowest-volatility crosses available, which is why a 185bp differential produces a carry-to-volatility ratio above 0.3. The only structural asymmetry disclosed in the payload is that the gated store found zero resistance zones and nine support zones meeting its two-touch threshold, which the store itself flags as a shortfall requiring round-number supplementation. That is an asymmetry worth recording but it is not a four-week directional stance, and placing levels on it is the second pass's work, not this one's. Neutral at low confidence is the honest output.

The estimated term structure is close to flat and very slightly inverted between 36.7 and 99.7 days at 5.576% and 5.476%, which signals an event premium at the front rather than a medium-term event being priced, and the absolute level remains low enough that the cross is cheap to hold in either direction. expression_assessment.vol_landscape_summary: AUD/NZD is intrinsically one of the lowest-volatility crosses in the G10, with realised sixty-day volatility of 4.73% against an estimated three-month implied of 5.476%. Both figures sit below either leg's volatility against the dollar, because the two currencies share most of their global drivers and the cross strips those out. The implied figure is a triangle estimate built from a realised correlation of 0.7833 rather than a quote, and the method is known to run low, so the true variance risk premium is probably wider than the stated 0.75 of a point. The practical consequence is that a 185bp differential buys an unusually good carry-to-volatility ratio of roughly 0.34, and that the cross is cheap to hold for the time a convergence thesis needs. (Pass-2 payload: realised volatility is 3.67% on 20 days and 4.48% on 60 days, below the 4.73% the verdict carried, putting carry-to-realised at 0.41–0.50.)

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For a non-dollar cross the question is not whether the dollar is strong but whether the two legs are differentially exposed to it, and they are, modestly and structurally in the base leg's favour. The backdrop is a firm dollar without funding stress: the broad dollar index at 120.33 is at the 67th percentile of its one-year range and up 1.88 points on the month, the US ten-year at 5.24% is at the top of its range, SOFR is inside the target range with reserves at roughly USD 2.93trn, quantitative tightening has ended and the Fed is buying bills, and central bank swap line usage is negligible. Both Antipodean currencies underperform at the US-exceptionalism end of the dollar smile, so the generalised effect cancels. What does not cancel is depth and backstop: the RBNZ has no standing Fed swap line, New Zealand's market is roughly a third of Australia's by futures open interest, and New Zealand must fund a persistent external deficit in a currency with thinner offshore bid. Australian banks also fund offshore, which is a genuine counterweight, but they do so in deeper markets with a triple-A sovereign behind them. On the cross specifically, the CME calendar roll premium of -146.7bp against a 185bp policy differential implies roughly 38bp of negative basis, a modest but real cost to funding the base leg against the quote leg. The net is a mild and structural pair-positive, scored at low confidence because it is an inference from market structure rather than from a quoted basis.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the dollar channel loses even the modest bilateral content it has tactically. The supply side of dollar liquidity is unambiguously easing: the Fed's balance sheet is expanding by roughly USD 17bn a month, reserves at USD 2.93trn are far above the scarcity threshold that produced the 2019 dislocation, and the Committee has committed to maintaining ample reserves and to buying bills. That is the configuration in which funding stress does not occur, and without stress the differential-backstop argument that gives the base leg a tactical edge simply does not activate. The dollar's rate advantage persists on the Fed's own median dot of 4.1% for both end-2026 and end-2027, but a dollar parked at the exceptionalism end of the smile penalises both Antipodean legs in roughly equal measure. The one seasonal item inside the window, year-end dollar funding demand around the December turn, affects both legs and marginally more the one without a swap line, but that is a tail rather than a path. With the generalised effect cancelling and the differential effect dormant absent stress, Neutral is the correct strategic output and the weight has been cut to 0.08 to reflect how little a dollar factor can say about a trans-Tasman cross.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.2999 on a minus-one to plus-one scale is a clear Bullish reading for the pair, meaning AUD/NZD rising, and it sits in the middle of the conviction-3 band. But the composition matters more than the number: four of ten factors carry the entire score and six are Neutral, so 40% of the tactical weight is doing all the work and the remaining 60% is genuinely silent. Policy and Rates contributes +0.1456 and Inflation and Growth +0.0864, together 77% of the total, and both rest on the same underlying observation, that the Australian leg's next policy step is discounted at roughly 20% while the New Zealand leg's is discounted at roughly 75%. This is therefore a depth reading, not a breadth reading, and it is one-mechanism deep. There is no offsetting negative at all on this horizon, which is itself worth flagging: a score with no bearish factor is a score with no internal hedge, and the single release that would remove it is the Australian September-quarter trimmed mean on 28 October.
tactical.rationale: At the applied tactical weights the verdict is decided by Policy and Rates at 0.28 and Inflation and Growth at 0.18, which between them carry 46% of the weight and 77% of the score, with Guidance at 0.07 and a reduced USD Liquidity at 0.07 supplying the remainder. The mechanism common to all four is a pricing asymmetry rather than a fundamental one: the bilateral policy differential is +185bp, the widest in the dollar bloc, and the modal four-week path narrows it because the RBNZ's 28 October move to 3.00% is roughly 75% discounted while the RBA's 3 November move is only roughly 20% discounted. Running the dossiers' own probabilities, 70% and 45% respectively, gives an expected realised compression of about 6.25bp against about 13.75bp priced, so the surprise asymmetry favours the pair rising even though the central path does not. The base and quote dossiers reinforce each other here rather than conflict: the base is standalone Bullish at +0.3040 and the quote standalone Bearish at -0.1593, which is the one configuration that amplifies rather than mutes a cross signal. The bilateral factors that modify the standalone views are the core inflation gap of roughly 90bp on the measures each bank targets, 3.6% trimmed mean against 2.7% sectoral factor core, and the 100bp unemployment gap, 4.6% against 5.6%, both of which say the base leg's central bank has more reason to keep moving. What is priced and what we expect diverge in exactly one measurable place, the probability attached to the Australian 3 November decision, and that is the whole of the edge. Everything else is deliberately Neutral: the commodity complex offsets inside four weeks with oil retracing against both legs' interests, positioning is short both currencies with the base leg's own data self-contradictory, the two legs share a risk beta, and the cross's structure is not visible to this pass by design. The path of least resistance is therefore upward but shallow, and the carry of roughly 15 to 19 pips a month is a real part of the four-week return rather than a rounding error on a cross whose realised volatility is 4.73%. The dated catalysts are New Zealand's September-quarter CPI on 21 October, the RBNZ Monetary Policy Review and Australia's September-quarter CPI both on 28 October, and the RBA decision on 3 November, which sits just beyond a strict four-week window but drives positioning within it. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because the thesis is one release wide: a soft Australian trimmed mean on 28 October removes it in a single print, and the score has no bearish factor to cushion that. It is 3 rather than 2 because the positive factors share one well-identified mechanism, the carry is genuinely payable while waiting, and both standalone dossiers point the same way. Pass-2 view (does not alter the score): the price payload makes us more cautious than the score on how to implement it. Spot is at the 94th percentile of its closing range, has made four lower daily highs since 22 September, and absorbed the RBA's 29 September hike with a flat close. We still accept the direction, but reward-to-risk at spot is worse than the factor composition implies, so the long should be built on dips rather than chased.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.2344 is a clear Bearish reading for the pair, meaning AUD/NZD falling, and it sits in the conviction-3 band. The composition is better balanced than the tactical score: three factors are Bearish for a combined -0.2933, two are Bullish for +0.0589, and five are Neutral covering 30% of the weight. Policy and Rates at -0.1431 and External Balance at -0.0950 supply 86% of the negative, and they are genuinely independent mechanisms, a convergence of policy paths and a divergence of real exchange rates and external positions, which is a stronger structure than a score of the same size resting on one channel. The honest caveat is that Guidance at -0.0552 is partly correlated with Policy and Rates, which is why its confidence was held at 46 rather than scored on its own merits; stripping it entirely would still leave -0.1792 and a Bearish stance. The score should be read as directionally reliable and magnitudinally soft, because roughly 77bp of the convergence it depends on is already visible in the 2-year differential.
strategic.rationale: At the applied strategic weights Policy and Rates at 0.27, External Balance at 0.19 and Guidance at 0.12 carry 58% of the weight and effectively all of the signal. The dominant mechanism is convergence: the RBNZ is early in a cycle that began from 2.25% in July with a published track peaking at 3.28% and bank paths running to 3.25-3.50% by March 2027, while the RBA at 4.60% is at or near a peak constrained by 4.6% unemployment and NAB business conditions negative for the first time since September 2020. The modal path narrows the differential from 185bp toward 135-160bp, and the gated calendar supplies the mechanism and the dates: RBNZ 28 October, RBA 3 November, RBA 8 December and RBNZ 9 December, with only the RBNZ's December meeting carrying a projection round and therefore a published track to revise upward. The second, independent mechanism is external: Australia runs the larger current account deficit at 3.67% of GDP with the balance on goods and services itself in deficit at AUD 5.1bn, against New Zealand's 3.2% and narrowing, and it does so with a real effective exchange rate of 116.11, the highest in the benchmarking set and up 9.97% over twelve months, against New Zealand's 102.84, flat on the year at the 44th percentile. World Bank purchasing power parity conversion factors put the cross roughly 15-18% expensive. The two standalone dossiers both score Neutral strategically, +0.0307 and -0.0658, which would naively imply a mildly rising pair, yet each independently nominates short AUD/NZD as its cleanest strategic expression; the bilateral factors that account for that gap are exactly the two above, neither of which shows up in a standalone score oriented against the dollar. What is priced is a great deal of this: the bilateral 2-year gap of roughly 106 to 108bp against a 185bp policy gap means the curve already discounts around 77bp of convergence, which is the principal reason confidence is 53 rather than 65 and the principal argument against the view. The edge is therefore in the speed of delivery rather than the direction, and the delivery risk skews toward faster compression because only one of the two banks has a scheduled vehicle to formalise a higher path. The two Bullish offsets are real but second-order: a New Zealand general election on 7 November and a post-election fiscal update in December against an Australian calendar with neither, and a 27-point net debt gap with a one-notch ratings advantage at two of three agencies. The path of least resistance is a drift lower in the cross rather than a break, and the conviction drivers are that the two negative mechanisms are independent and well evidenced, offset by the fact that the market has already done most of the work in the front end. Conviction is 3, not 4, for that reason and because a Chinese stimulus package resetting iron ore is a single identifiable event that would flip Factor 5.

consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish the pair over one to three months at conviction 3, net weighted score -0.2344, driven by policy-path convergence from 185bp toward 135-160bp and by a real exchange rate and external balance divergence that favours the quote leg.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Strategically in line with the bank view on the cross, which is also directionally bearish (though we are less bearish than the most aggressive house); tactically opposed to it, because that view is a convergence thesis with no four-week pricing content.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Tactical: our 1M expected rate of 1.2450 is 300–450 pips above the Q4 consensus and BofA levels; we are opposed on timing, not on destination. Strategic: our 6M base of 1.2150 is about 60 pips below the aggregator's Q1 2027 figure of 1.2213, about 50 pips below RBC's 1.22 and about 350 pips above BofA's 1.18.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The convergence case for a lower cross is sound and we hold it strategically, but as published it rests heavily on where the cross has recently traded, specifically its position near the top of its 52-week range, and that is precisely the kind of evidence this pass refuses. Stripping it out leaves two admissible pillars: the policy-path differential and the valuation and external-balance gap. Both survive scrutiny strategically. Neither has four-week content, and over four weeks the admissible evidence points the other way, because the compression leg of the convergence is already 75% discounted while the expansion leg is only 20% discounted, and because the carry of roughly 15 to 19 pips a month is paid to the side the convergence thesis says to be short. We also weigh the already-discounted portion of the convergence more heavily than the consensus view appears to: a bilateral 2-year gap of roughly 108bp against a 185bp policy gap means the market has already done roughly 77bp of the work, which caps the strategic payoff and is why conviction is 3 rather than 4. One fact supports tactical caution about joining the short now: BofA's economists had expected the RBA to leave rates unchanged until the second half of 2027 while the RBNZ hiked twice more in 2026, and the RBA's unanimous 29 September hike has already broken the first half of that premise.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the tactical read is right, the pair rises into and through the 28 October cluster as Australian front-end rates reprice 10-18bp on an upside trimmed mean while the New Zealand leg has little room left, with carry accruing throughout on an unusually low-volatility cross. If the strategic read is right, the cross grinds lower as the RBNZ lifts its published track at the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement while the RBA has no scheduled vehicle to extend its own guidance, and the real exchange rate gap of 13 REER points begins to close. Payoff if right on the strategic view is about 240 pips gross (about 150 net of carry).
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: The tactical risk is concentrated in one release: a soft Australian September-quarter trimmed mean on 28 October removes the entire pricing asymmetry in a single print, and the tactical score has no bearish factor to cushion it. The strategic risk is that convergence is already so well discounted in the 2-year differential that delivery produces no further move, and that a Chinese stimulus package out of the December Central Economic Work Conference resets iron ore, restoring the terms-of-trade support whose absence Factor 5 assumes. A weekly close through 1.2620 would mean the RBA is still hiking.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons are genuinely opposed and the opposition is mechanical rather than a judgement conflict. The same 185bp differential drives both, but over four weeks what matters is how each leg's next step is discounted, and the compression leg is 75% priced while the expansion leg is 20% priced, so the surprise asymmetry favours the pair rising. Over one to three months what matters is the trajectory, and the trajectory narrows the differential while the external and valuation gaps work in the same direction. Three factors change sign between horizons and each for a stated reason: Policy and Rates because pricing gives way to trajectory, External Balance because quarterly commodity shocks that offset inside four weeks give way to levels of current account and real exchange rate that do not, and Guidance because a gap between stated intention and market pricing gives way to the question of which bank has a scheduled projection round in which to formalise a new path.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 28 October to 3 November window. New Zealand's September-quarter CPI on 21 October and the Australian September-quarter CPI and RBNZ Monetary Policy Review both on 28 October resolve the tactical pricing asymmetry, and the RBA decision on 3 November consumes the last of it. From that point only the trajectory remains, and the first scheduled test of it is the pair of decisions one day apart on 8 and 9 December, of which only the RBNZ's carries a Monetary Policy Statement and a new published track.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the two horizons as separate propositions rather than one view with a long hold. The tactical case is a short-dated, catalyst-dependent proposition that resolves on a known date and should not be carried past 3 November, because after that the factor that generated it has been consumed and the strategic factors take over with the opposite sign. The strategic case is a slow convergence proposition on a cross whose low realised volatility makes it cheap to hold, with the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement as the first scheduled confirmation. Pass-2 implementation: run the tactical long from 1.2390/1.2305 with a daily-close stop below 1.2185, flat by the 4 November close. Initiate the strategic short only after that, selling 1.2460–1.2500 or a daily close below 1.2290, with a weekly-close stop above 1.2620. Never hold both at once. The one scenario that removes both views together is a soft Australian trimmed mean on 28 October: it stops out the long and starts the short early, in which case the strategic short may be entered on the 28 October close below 1.2290.
